member.summary: The descriptor-indexing features an adapter may implement without implementing all of them, each answered as the adapter reported it.

remarks.para: Descriptor indexing is one extension but thirteen feature bits, and a conforming adapter is allowed to set any subset. The backend needs seven of them together for a bindless heap to work at all -- that decision is -- and these are the six it does not depend on, which are therefore requested one by one, each only where it was found.

The RTX 3080 the port was written against has all thirteen, which is why the same code ran there.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Vulkan.Capabilities.VulkanCapabilityProbe
member.summary: Asks an adapter what it can do, and later asks the logical device to turn exactly that on.

remarks.para: The two halves belong together. Whatever the probe reports as available is what device creation must enable, field for field: enabling a feature the adapter does not have fails device creation outright, and leaving one off that was reported available means a shader compiled against it faults at the first dispatch. Keeping the query and the enable in one type is what stops the two lists drifting.

Both halves build the same shape of pNext chain, conditionally: a structure is linked only when the extension that defines it is present, because linking a structure type the driver does not know is undefined rather than politely ignored.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Vulkan.Capabilities.VulkanDeviceCapabilities
member.summary: What the chosen adapter can actually do: every optional feature the backend asked for, answered, and the limits that go with the ones it got.

remarks.para: An extension being present is not the same as a feature being usable. Vulkan splits the two: the extension string says the driver carries the code, and a feature bit read through vkGetPhysicalDeviceFeatures2 says this adapter actually implements it. Enabling an extension whose feature bit is false is legal and then fails at the first call, so every capability here is decided by the pair — string present and bit set — which is the only check that means anything.

The limits travel with the flags because they are needed far from where they were read: a shader binding table's record stride is computed from the ray-tracing handle size and alignment, and a descriptor heap's stride from the descriptor buffer's own alignment. Reading them once at selection and carrying them means those decisions never re-query the physical device.

member.summary: Builds a Vulkan pNext chain of extension structures whose addresses stay valid for as long as the chain is alive.

remarks.para: Vulkan extends a structure by linking further structures off its pNext pointer, and every one of them must still be at the address it was linked at when the call is made. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Vulkan.Memory.VulkanAllocator
member.summary: Chooses which of the adapter's memory types an allocation lives in, and makes the allocation.

remarks.para: Vulkan hands memory management to the application: every buffer and image is backed by memory the caller allocates and binds itself, and the caller alone knows whether a resource wants to live where the GPU reaches it fastest () or where the CPU can write it (). This concentrates the type search and the allocation so every resource asks the same way.

One is allocated per resource here. That is the simple, correct starting point; a driver caps how many allocations may exist at once, so a later pass sub-allocates many resources out of a few large blocks. Keeping every allocation behind this one seam is what lets that pass be a change here rather than everywhere.

A freed block is retained rather than returned to the driver, keyed by the shape it was allocated for (memory type, byte size, whether it carries a device address), and the next allocation of that same shape is handed a retained block instead of calling vkAllocateMemory again. A fresh host-visible allocation is a blocking driver call of tens to hundreds of milliseconds — the terrain streams growing pages in and out as the camera turns, and re-using a retired page's memory turns that per-page stall into a dictionary lookup. Retained memory is capped so the pool cannot grow without bound; over the cap a freed block is genuinely returned.

The size in that key is rounded up rather than exact, and that is what makes the pool work at all for anything but the terrain. Pages are one size and hit an exact-size pool every time; a level's thousand textures are a thousand different sizes and hit it never — so swapping a menu backdrop was a thousand vkAllocateMemory calls against a thousand vkFreeMemory calls, measured at 794 ms allocating and 868 ms freeing over a handful of swaps, all of it on the render thread. Rounding to three significant binary digits (see ) puts eight buckets in every power of two: an eighth wasted at worst, and a texture the outgoing level freed fits the incoming one's.

Host-visible memory is pooled under a cap of its own, and a small one. It is the memory that counts against the process: a block of it parked in the pool is RAM the game holds and does not use. One shared cap let a level's worth of upload staging -- every texture of a menu backdrop passes through some -- fill the whole pool and stay there, while the device-local blocks that are the reason the pool exists were freed for want of room. Each kind now has its own ceiling, and gives the host-visible blocks back once a load is over.

member.summary: A Vulkan buffer and the device memory backing it.

remarks.para: A buffer is created, its memory requirements read, memory of a suitable type allocated, and the two bound together — the four steps every Vulkan buffer needs, kept in one place so a caller names only the size, what the buffer is for, and whether the CPU must be able to write it.

A host-visible buffer can be written straight from the CPU and is what staging uploads and per-frame uniform data use; a device-local buffer lives in the memory the GPU reads fastest and is filled by copying from a host-visible staging buffer. This type covers both — the difference is only which memory properties it was asked for — and mapping is available exactly when the memory is host visible.

Two further things a modern buffer carries. A persistent mapping stays mapped for the buffer's whole life rather than being mapped and unmapped around each write, which is what data rewritten every frame wants: mapping is not free and doing it per write on a per-frame buffer is pure overhead. A device address turns the buffer into a raw pointer a shader can dereference and a build command can be pointed at, which is how acceleration structures reach their geometry and how a descriptor heap is bound — neither is expressible through a descriptor.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Vulkan.Rhi.VulkanRhiDevice
member.summary: Bind groups, submission, readback, and what this device reports about itself.
The RHI, answered through Vulkan.

remarks.para: Where the WebGPU implementation is mostly a translation followed by one call, this one has work to do: the interface promises no barriers and no layouts, and Vulkan has both. What that costs is paid here and in the encoder, and it is the price of an interface a browser can also implement.
It owns nothing it did not make. The device, the allocator and the command pool are handed in, because the backend already has them and a second set would be a second set of everything.

member.summary: The frame: acquiring an image, submitting what was recorded into it, and presenting.

remarks.para: The interface has no swapchain, which is the point: it asks for the texture this frame draws into and says when the frame is over. Everything below — the rotation, the fences, the two semaphores that order an acquire against a present — is this backend's business and has no counterpart on the other.

Submissions made during a frame are held rather than sent, and go out as one submit when the frame ends. That is what lets the acquire semaphore be waited on once and the present semaphore be signalled once, which is the ordering a swapchain needs and which the interface's own Submit cannot express.

member.summary: The raster half: graphics pipelines, built without a render pass object.

remarks.para: Through dynamic rendering, which is what makes the interface's render pass implementable at all. The interface states its attachments when the pass begins, the way WebGPU does; classic Vulkan wants a render pass object and a framebuffer built in advance from the same information, and keeping those in step with attachments that change per frame is a cache and an invalidation rule and a source of bugs. Dynamic rendering takes the attachments directly, so there is nothing to keep in step.
It is Vulkan 1.3, and a device without it is refused rather than served by a second path. Two ways of beginning a pass would be two ways for the picture to differ.

member.summary: The device's side of Streamline: the capability, and the frame's end it hooks into.
member.remarks: Three things Streamline needs of the frame that nothing else does. Textures frame generation reads at present time are put back into the layout their tags named before the image is presented; the present is bracketed by the latency markers and carries the frame's index as its id; and frame generation's signal that it has finished with a frame's inputs is waited on by the next submit.
member.summary: Buffer writes queued ahead of the next submission, and what every submission holds until the GPU is done.

remarks.para: Writes. The interface's WriteBuffer is WebGPU's queue.writeBuffer: it lands before any work submitted after it, and nobody waits for it. It used to be a submission of its own, waited on -- hundreds a frame, each a round trip to the GPU, which left the renderer spending most of its frame asleep. Now the bytes go into a staging chunk and the copy into an upload command buffer, which goes to the queue first in the next submission, ending in a barrier that makes it visible to everything after it.

Lifetimes. A command buffer and a staging chunk are freed only once the submission that carried them has finished: inside a frame that is the frame's fence, waited on when its slot comes round; outside one, a fence of the submission's own. Before this, every encoder's command buffer and every frame's present transition were allocated and never freed at all.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Vulkan.Streamline.StreamlineVulkanLoader
member.summary: Binds Silk's Vulkan API to Streamline's interposer instead of the system loader.

remarks.para: Streamline has to see a handful of Vulkan calls go past — instance and device creation, so it can add the extensions, features and queues its plugins need, and the swapchain and present calls, which is what makes frame generation possible at all. There are two ways to arrange that. The manual route hooks each of those entry points by hand and hands Streamline the device afterwards through slSetVulkanInfo. The other is to load sl.interposer.dll in place of vulkan-1.dll and let it forward everything it does not care about.

The second is taken here, and it is barely any code: the interposer exports the whole Vulkan 1.0-1.3 core plus the surface and swapchain entry points, so it is a drop-in replacement for the loader, and Silk resolves extension functions through vkGetDeviceProcAddr — which it now gets from the interposer, so those come back proxied too without anything asking for it. Nothing in the rest of the backend changes, and there is no list of hooked functions to keep in step with a future SDK.

The one thing this does not cover is the window surface. Silk creates that through GLFW, which loads Vulkan itself, so vkCreateWin32SurfaceKHR goes past Streamline unseen. Nothing in the production plugins hooks surface creation — frame generation and Reflex hook the swapchain, which does come through here — so the only thing missed is the development overlay's own window hook.

member.remarks: This mirrors Silk's own Vk.GetApi exactly, and deliberately so — the only difference is which library the first context loads. member.summary: The graphics command pool, and the one-off submissions that stand outside the frame loop.

remarks.para: Every command the backend issues is recorded into a command buffer allocated from a pool tied to the graphics family. The per-frame buffers the frame loop owns come from here; so do the short-lived buffers that upload a texture or transition an image, which do not belong to any frame and are submitted on their own through .

submits and then waits: it is for load-time work — staging a mesh, building a mip chain, moving an image to its first layout — where the simplicity of a synchronous copy is worth more than the pipelining a fence-and-poll would keep. Nothing on the frame path uses it.

is the same work without the per-item wait. A submit-and-wait costs a queue round trip whatever it carries, and a level's worth of textures is hundreds of them: measured over a menu session, six hundred milliseconds of the render thread went on vkWaitForFences waiting for copies that together took a fraction of that. Batched, they accumulate into one buffer and pay one round trip between them. The batch is flushed before anything else is submitted, so the queue runs it first and anything after it sees what it wrote; the flush itself does not wait, and the staging it held is released once its fence has signalled.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Vulkan.VulkanSwapchain
member.summary: The swapchain: the small ring of images the compositor shows, and everything decided to create it — the surface format, the present mode, and the extent.

remarks.para: A swapchain is the one part of the backend the window's size reaches into, so it is also the one part rebuilt while the program runs: a resize, a move to another monitor, or a minimise leaves the old chain out of date, and the fix is to wait for the device to go idle and make a new chain against the same surface. Everything that depends on the extent — the image views here, and the framebuffers and per-image targets above — is rebuilt with it.

The format is chosen as an unsigned-normalised B8G8R8A8, matching the engine's own Bgra32 pixel and the OpenGL backend's default framebuffer: the engine tone maps and encodes its own output, so a swapchain that re-encoded to sRGB a second time would double the gamma. The present mode follows the v-sync request — FIFO when it is on, since every driver has it, and mailbox or immediate when it is off so a frame need not wait for the blank.
